subsection: Emergence and spread of infectious disease

notes.h: Key terms: emerging, endemic, epidemic and pandemic
notes.b: Disease specialists use precise words for how common a disease is and how fast it is changing. You need these terms to describe any outbreak, and they appear throughout the rest of this subsection.
points: An emerging infectious disease is one that has newly appeared in a population, or one that was known but is rapidly increasing in incidence (the number of new cases) or in geographic range.
A re-emerging disease is one that had declined and is increasing again, e.g. measles where vaccination rates fall, or TB with drug-resistant strains.
Endemic means always present at a fairly steady level in a region, so the number of cases is predictable from year to year.
An epidemic, or outbreak, is a sudden increase in cases above the expected level in a region.
A pandemic is an epidemic that spreads across several continents or worldwide, e.g. COVID-19, which the World Health Organization declared a pandemic on 11 March 2020.
notes.tip: Learn the order of scale: endemic (steady), epidemic (sudden rise in a region), pandemic (several continents or worldwide). Examiners expect each term used precisely, with an example.

notes.h: Key terms: zoonosis, reservoir and carrier
notes.b: Some terms describe where a pathogen (a disease-causing organism) lives between outbreaks and who can pass it on. These explain why some diseases are so hard to get rid of.
points: A zoonosis is an infectious disease that passes from animals to humans, e.g. avian influenza or rabies.
Most emerging human diseases are zoonoses, often from wild animals, because people have little immunity to pathogens they have never met. There is more on this in Emerging diseases and society.
A reservoir is a host population in which a pathogen persists and from which it infects others, e.g. badgers for bovine TB in Ireland, or wild birds for avian influenza.
A carrier is an infected individual who shows no symptoms but can pass on the pathogen, so nobody knows to avoid them.
notes.tip: Keep the two terms apart: a reservoir is a whole host population that keeps the pathogen going, while a carrier is one infected individual with no symptoms.

notes.h: How infectious diseases are transmitted
notes.b: A pathogen can only cause an outbreak if it can get from one host to the next. There are several routes, and each has typical diseases that use it, in both animals and plants.
points: Airborne droplets and aerosols (tiny particles hanging in the air) from coughs, sneezes and breath spread influenza, TB, measles and COVID-19.
Wind-borne spores spread ash dieback, cereal rusts and potato blight in plants, because spores are light enough to be carried between fields.
Direct contact, touch and skin to skin, spreads ringworm and athlete's foot.
Indirect contact via contaminated objects and surfaces (fomites), hands, tools and clothing spreads disease. In plants, contact with hands and tools spreads tobacco mosaic virus.
Contaminated food and water, the faecal–oral route (pathogens in faeces reach the mouth), spreads cholera, Salmonella food poisoning and amoebic dysentery.
Body fluids spread HIV and hepatitis B through sexual contact, blood (shared needles and unscreened transfusions) and mother to baby.

Vectors are animals that carry pathogens between hosts: mosquitoes (malaria), ticks (Lyme disease), tsetse flies (sleeping sickness), elm bark beetles (Dutch elm disease), aphids (many plant viruses, e.g. barley yellow dwarf virus) and biting midges (bluetongue virus of sheep and cattle).

In plants, rain splash, soil, infected seed, tubers and cuttings also spread disease. Vegetative propagation (growing new plants from parts of old ones) passes viruses and blight to the next crop, and grafting does too.
notes.tip: When asked how a disease spreads, name the route and give a matching example, in plants as well as animals. Remember that a vector is an animal that carries the pathogen between hosts.

notes.h: Local and regional spread of organisms
notes.b: Diseases spread when infected organisms, or the things they touch, move. Over short distances this happens through everyday contact, and over a whole country it follows the trade and travel routes of animals and people.
points: Local spread occurs within a household, school, hospital or farm, between neighbouring fields by wind and rain splash, and between neighbouring farms by animals straying, shared equipment, vehicles and people's boots.

Regional spread occurs when farm animals move through marts (livestock markets) and between farms, when plants and animals are traded within a country or the EU, when wild animals move seasonally, and when people commute and holiday.
In the 2001 foot-and-mouth disease epidemic in Britain, infected sheep were moved through markets across the country before the disease was detected, spreading it to many farms.
Control of that epidemic needed a ban on animal movement and the culling of millions of animals, which shows how costly it is once movement has carried a disease widely.
notes.tip: For a regional example use the 2001 foot-and-mouth epidemic in Britain: sheep moved through markets before detection, so the disease reached many farms.

notes.h: Global spread of organisms
notes.b: Modern travel and trade mean a pathogen no longer stays where it started. A disease can reach another continent before anyone knows it is there.
points: Air travel can carry an infected person to any continent within a day, faster than many diseases take to show symptoms, so travellers can carry infection without knowing it.
COVID-19 reached every continent within months of its first identification in Wuhan, China, in December 2019.
International trade moves pathogens and vectors in plants, wood, soil, live animals and goods. Ash dieback spread through Europe partly in imported young ash plants and was found in Ireland in 2012.
The second, more aggressive epidemic of Dutch elm disease reached Britain from the late 1960s in imported elm logs.
The Asian tiger mosquito (Aedes albopictus), a vector of several viruses, has spread to many countries in used tyres and plants.
Migrating wild birds carry avian influenza between continents, because infected birds fly long distances without any border controls.
notes.tip: Say that COVID-19 was first identified in Wuhan. Don't state its origin, because that is still debated.

notes.h: The pet and wildlife trade: chytrid fungus
notes.b: Trade in live animals can move a disease into places where the local species have never met it. Amphibians show how serious this can be.
points: The pet and wildlife trade spread chytrid fungus (Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis) around the world in the trade in amphibians.
Chytrid is linked to the decline of hundreds of amphibian species and the extinction of some.

notes.h: Factor 1: how long a pathogen persists in a host
notes.b: Emergence and spread depend on several interrelated factors, and the first is persistence. The longer a host carries a pathogen in a way that can pass on, the more chances it has to infect others.
points: The longer a host is infectious, the more others it can infect.
Persistence includes long infectious periods, carriers without symptoms, latent infections (the pathogen is present but inactive) that reactivate, and reservoir hosts.
HIV may cause no symptoms for years while the person can still pass it on.
Herpes viruses stay latent in nerve cells for life, so the person is never rid of the virus. There is more on this in Viruses: replication.
TB bacteria can stay dormant (inactive) in the lungs for years and become active later.
notes.tip: Link persistence to spread: a long infectious period, or a carrier with no symptoms, means more people are exposed. Mary Mallon is the usual named human example.

notes.h: Persistence: examples in people, animals and plants
notes.b: Persistence shows up in each kind of host, from a single healthy-looking person to wildlife and crops.
points: Mary Mallon, known as Typhoid Mary, was born in Co. Tyrone in 1869 and worked as a cook in New York. She carried the typhoid bacterium, Salmonella Typhi, without symptoms and infected many of the families she cooked for.
Health authorities isolated her for most of the rest of her life, because as a carrier she could not be identified by illness.
Bovine TB persists in Irish cattle partly because badgers act as a wildlife reservoir that reinfects herds, so clearing the disease from cattle alone is not enough.
Plant viruses persist in perennial plants (which live for years), weeds and tubers, so infected seed potatoes carry viruses into the next year's crop.
Phytophthora infestans, the cause of potato blight, survives the winter in infected tubers left in the ground or in dumps.
notes.tip: Potato blight is caused by Phytophthora infestans, a water mould, not a fungus or a virus.

notes.h: Factor 2: mutations produce new variants
notes.b: A mutation is a random change in a pathogen's genetic material. Pathogens that reproduce quickly produce huge numbers of changed copies, so some will spread better than the original.
points: Pathogens with short generation times and large populations produce many mutants, because each new copy is another chance for a change.
RNA viruses mutate fastest because their copying enzyme doesn't proofread (check for copying errors). There is more on this in Viruses: replication.

Antigenic drift: small mutations gradually change a virus's surface antigens (the molecules the immune system recognises), so memory cells and antibodies from earlier infections or vaccines no longer fit well.
Antigenic drift is why influenza returns every winter and why flu vaccines are updated each year.
Mutations likewise produced new SARS-CoV-2 variants, such as Delta and Omicron, that spread faster or partly escaped immunity, causing new waves of COVID-19.
notes.tip: When explaining why flu returns each winter, name antigenic drift: the surface antigens change a little, so existing immunity fits poorly.

notes.h: Mutations: antigenic shift and host jumps
notes.b: Mutations can also change what a pathogen is able to do, giving it a new host or defeating a crop's defences.
points: Antigenic shift (influenza): if two different flu viruses infect the same cell, e.g. in a pig, their RNA segments can mix to form a new strain with surface antigens that no human population has met.
Antigenic shift has caused flu pandemics, e.g. the 2009 H1N1 (swine flu) pandemic, because with no existing immunity the new strain spreads easily.
Mutations can let a pathogen infect a new host species (spillover, e.g. a bird virus gaining the ability to infect mammals), become more transmissible, or overcome resistance bred into crops.
The Ug99 strain of wheat stem rust, identified in Uganda in 1999, overcame resistance genes used in most of the world's wheat varieties.
notes.tip: Don't mix up drift and shift: drift is gradual small mutations, while shift is a sudden new strain made by mixing RNA segments from two flu viruses in one cell.

notes.h: Factor 3: how antibiotic or chemical resistance arises
notes.b: Resistance means a pathogen or pest survives a drug or chemical that used to kill it. It arises by natural selection (survival of the individuals best suited to their conditions), which happens in four steps. There is more on this in The theory of evolution by natural selection.
points: 1. Random mutations, or genes passed between bacteria on plasmids (small rings of DNA), make a few individuals resistant.
2. The antibiotic or chemical kills the susceptible individuals.
3. The resistant survivors reproduce with less competition.
4. The next generation is mostly resistant. The chemical doesn't cause the mutation; it selects it.
notes.tip: Say that antibiotics select resistant bacteria and never that they cause the mutation. Bacteria become resistant, not people.

notes.h: What speeds up resistance, and examples
notes.b: Resistance appears wherever a drug or chemical is used, but some practices make it spread faster. The examples cover people, crops and livestock.
points: Overuse and misuse of antibiotics speed up resistance: use for viral infections (which antibiotics cannot treat), not finishing courses, and use in farm animals.
Poor infection control in hospitals and heavy repeated use of one pesticide also speed up resistance.
MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) is resistant to many antibiotics and spreads in hospitals.
Multidrug-resistant TB, malaria parasites resistant to some antimalarial drugs, and mosquitoes resistant to insecticides, which weakens malaria control.
Fungi that cause crop diseases are resistant to some fungicides, and parasitic worms of sheep and cattle are resistant to some anthelmintics (drugs that kill worms).
Resistant pathogens persist longer in hosts and spread further, linking factors 1 and 3.
notes.tip: For explain-how-resistance-spreads questions, link overuse of a drug to selection of resistant survivors, then to those survivors spreading.

notes.h: Factor 4: immunity level in the population
notes.b: A pathogen needs susceptible hosts, meaning individuals with no immunity to it. How many of these there are in a population strongly affects how far and how fast an outbreak goes.
points: A pathogen spreads only if it can reach susceptible (non-immune) hosts. The higher the proportion of immune individuals, the fewer susceptible hosts there are and the slower the spread. This is herd immunity. There is more on this in Acquired immunity, prevention and treatment.
A pathogen new to a population meets no immunity at all, so it spreads fast and can be very severe, e.g. COVID-19 in 2020, before vaccines.
Smallpox and measles, brought by Europeans to the Americas from the late 1400s, killed very large numbers of Indigenous people, who had never been exposed to them.
Immunity falls when vaccination rates drop, as when measles outbreaks return.

Immunity also falls when protection from vaccination or infection wanes over time, and where many people have weakened immune systems, e.g. from untreated HIV or malnutrition, or the very young and very old.
notes.tip: Give both sides: more immune people means slower spread, and falling vaccination or a brand-new pathogen means faster spread.

notes.h: Immunity in plants: genetic uniformity and the Great Famine
notes.b: Plants have no antibody-based immunity like animals, but the same principle applies. What matters is whether any individuals in the crop can resist the pathogen.
points: In plants, the equivalent is genetic uniformity. A monoculture (a crop of one genetically identical variety) has no resistant individuals, so a pathogen that infects one plant can infect them all.
In Ireland in the 1840s, most of the poor depended on one potato variety, the Lumper, grown from tubers (genetically identical clones) and susceptible to blight.
When Phytophthora infestans arrived in 1845, crops failed across the country in successive years. About one million people died and over a million emigrated in the Great Famine.
notes.tip: Give the famine as the 1840s with blight arriving in 1845, never a single year, and use only 'about one million' died. Explain it through genetic uniformity: one susceptible clone, so no resistant plants.

notes.h: Factor 5: mobility in affected populations
notes.b: The more infected hosts move and mix, the more other hosts they meet, so the further a pathogen travels. Mobility applies to people, livestock, wildlife and vectors.
points: The more infected hosts move and mix, the more contacts each has and the further the pathogen spreads. The routes are those in local, regional and global spread above.
Crowding in cities, refugee camps, festivals and mass gatherings, travel and migration, and the movement of livestock all increase spread.
Migration of wild animals, such as birds, also moves pathogens into new areas.
Vector mobility: climate warming lets vectors survive further north and for longer each year, carrying disease into new regions.
Bluetongue, a midge-borne virus of sheep and cattle, spread into northern Europe from 2006.

Reducing mobility reduces spread: animal movement bans in foot-and-mouth outbreaks, travel restrictions and quarantine in human epidemics, and import controls on plants. There is more on this in Emerging diseases and society.
notes.tip: Use the control measures as evidence for mobility: if banning movement slows an outbreak, then movement was driving it.

notes.h: Factor 6: the basic reproduction number, R₀
notes.b: To compare outbreaks and predict whether one will grow, scientists use a single number, R₀. It measures how contagious a pathogen is when nobody has immunity.
points: The basic reproduction number, R₀ ('R nought'), is the average number of new (secondary) infections caused by one infected individual in a population where everyone is susceptible, with no immunity and no control measures.
R₀ greater than 1: each case causes more than one new case on average, so numbers grow and an epidemic can occur.
R₀ equal to 1: numbers stay steady, which is endemic.
R₀ less than 1: each case causes fewer than one new case, so the outbreak dies out.
notes.tip: Define R₀ exactly: secondary infections from one case in a fully susceptible population. It is not the total number infected, not the death rate and not the effective R. R₀ = 1 is the threshold, so growth needs R₀ greater than 1.

notes.h: R₀ worked examples
notes.b: Each infected person passes the pathogen to R₀ others, so cases multiply by R₀ every generation of infection (one round of people infecting the next). Working through numbers shows why R₀ above or below 1 matters.
points: Growth example: with R₀ = 2, one case leads to 2, then 4, then 8, then 16 new cases per generation of infection. After 10 generations, one case has led to 2¹⁰ = 1,024 new cases in that generation.
Decline example: with R₀ = 0.5, 100 cases give 50, then 25, then about 12, and the outbreak fades.
Diagram: a branching tree from one case, giving 2, then 4, then 8 cases (R₀ = 2), beside a single chain with one case per generation (R₀ = 1). Label each generation.
notes.tip: Exams may ask you to calculate cases after several generations. Multiply by R₀ for each generation, so R₀ = 2 over 10 generations is 2¹⁰.

notes.h: What R₀ depends on
notes.b: R₀ is not a fixed property of a pathogen. It combines features of the pathogen, the host and the environment, which are the factors already covered.
points: R₀ depends on how long a host is infectious (persistence), so a longer infectious period raises R₀.
R₀ depends on how many contacts an infected host has per day (mobility and crowding), so more contacts raise R₀.
R₀ depends on the chance that a contact passes on the infection (the transmission route, and mutations that make a pathogen more transmissible).
So R₀ is not fixed for a disease: it differs between populations and settings.

notes.h: Effective reproduction number, R
notes.b: In real outbreaks some people are already immune or control measures are in place. The effective reproduction number measures spread under those real conditions.
points: The effective reproduction number, R (sometimes written Rt), is the average number of new infections per case at a given time, in a population where some people are immune or control measures are in place.
Approximately, R = R₀ × the proportion still susceptible. For example, R₀ = 3 with half the population immune gives R = 3 × 0.5 = 1.5.
Control aims to bring R below 1, so that each case infects fewer than one other person and the outbreak dies out.
notes.tip: Don't say R₀ changes when people get vaccinated. R₀ is for a fully susceptible population, and it is R that falls.

notes.h: Herd-immunity threshold
notes.b: If R₀ tells us how contagious a disease is, we can work out how many people must be immune to stop it spreading. The more contagious the disease, the higher that proportion.
points: Herd-immunity threshold: to stop sustained spread, the proportion immune must be at least 1 − 1/R₀.
Examples: R₀ = 2 needs 1 − ½ = 50% immune; R₀ = 4 needs 1 − ¼ = 75% immune; R₀ = 10 needs 90% immune.
Measles is one of the most contagious diseases, with R₀ usually quoted as 12–18, so about 95% of people must be immune.
The World Health Organization therefore recommends at least 95% coverage with two doses of measles vaccine.
notes.tip: Exams may ask you to calculate the proportion that must be immune. Use 1 − 1/R₀ and show the working.

notes.h: Assumptions of the R₀ model
notes.b: R₀ comes from a simple model, and a model is only as good as its assumptions. Real outbreaks differ in important ways.
points: The model's assumptions are that everyone is equally likely to meet everyone else and that R₀ stays constant. There is more on this in Models.
Real populations are clustered, behaviour changes during outbreaks and new variants change R₀, so estimates are updated as data come in.

notes.h: How the factors interact
notes.b: The six factors do not work one at a time. Real outbreaks happen when several combine, and other changes in how we live bring pathogens and new hosts into contact.
points: The factors act together, not one at a time. A mutation that makes a virus more transmissible raises R₀, and a population with low immunity and high mobility then lets it spread widely.
Long persistence in carriers lets a pathogen reach new areas undetected, and resistance to drugs lets infections last longer, raising R₀ further.
Plant example: a genetically uniform crop (low immunity), a pathogen spread by wind and trade (mobility) and survival in tubers (persistence) together explain the speed of the potato famine.

Other drivers increase contact between pathogens and new hosts: clearing forests and expanding farms into wild areas (more contact with wild animals), intensive farming of large numbers of genetically similar animals kept close together, climate change (vectors' ranges), poverty, poor sanitation, and conflict, which weakens health systems.
notes.tip: Questions ask you to explain how named factors contribute to a disease. Pick the factors, give a plant or animal example for each, and show how they combine.

keyTerms.definition: An infectious disease that has newly appeared in a population, or is rapidly increasing in incidence or geographic range.
Always present at a fairly steady level in a region.
An epidemic that spreads across several continents or worldwide.
An infectious disease that passes from animals to humans.
A host population in which a pathogen persists and from which it infects others.
Gradual change in a virus's surface antigens caused by small mutations, so earlier immunity fits less well.
A sudden change in a virus's surface antigens when RNA segments from two different flu viruses mix to form a new strain.
The average number of secondary infections caused by one case in a fully susceptible population with no control measures.
The average number of new infections per case at a given time, allowing for immunity and control measures.
The proportion of a population that must be immune, equal to 1 − 1/R₀, to stop sustained spread.

questions.prompt: What is meant by the reproduction number, R₀? Explain what happens to an outbreak when R₀ is greater than 1 and when it is less than 1.
questions.model: R₀ is the average number of new secondary infections caused by one infected individual in a population where everyone is susceptible, with no immunity and no control measures. When R₀ is greater than 1, each case causes more than one new case on average, so numbers grow and an epidemic can occur. When R₀ is less than 1, each case causes fewer than one new case, so the outbreak dies out.

questions.prompt: A disease has an R₀ of 4. (i) Calculate the percentage of the population that must be immune to prevent its spread. (ii) Explain why vaccinating this percentage protects people who are not vaccinated.
questions.model: (i) The herd-immunity threshold is 1 − 1/R₀ = 1 − 1/4 = 0.75, so 75% of the population must be immune. (ii) When 75% of people are immune, the pathogen can find too few susceptible hosts. Each case then causes on average no more than one new infection, so the effective reproduction number falls to 1 or below and spread cannot be sustained. People who are not vaccinated are protected indirectly, because the pathogen has few susceptible hosts to reach them.

questions.prompt: Explore how any three of the following factors contribute to the emergence of infectious diseases in plants and animals: persistence of the pathogen in a host, mutations, chemical resistance, the immunity level of the population, mobility.
questions.model: Persistence: a pathogen that survives in a host for a long time can infect many others. Phytophthora infestans survives the winter in infected potato tubers, so blight returns the next year, and TB bacteria can stay dormant in the lungs for years. Mutations: a changing pathogen escapes existing immunity or resistance. Antigenic drift changes influenza surface antigens each year, so flu vaccines must be updated, and the Ug99 strain of wheat stem rust overcame resistance genes used in most of the world's wheat. Immunity level: a population with low immunity lets a pathogen spread quickly. The Lumper potato, a genetically uniform crop, had no resistant plants, so blight spread through it and caused the Irish Great Famine, while measles outbreaks return where vaccination rates fall.
